When asked whether Hong Kong currently provides sufficient support for visually impaired students, Cheng expressed satisfaction, but noted that different types of visually impaired individuals have their own needs, and expressed hope that society could achieve greater inclusion. In addition, Cheng shared that the secret to achieving top marks lies in handwritten notes, which help deepen memory, complemented by AI assistance.

Cheng shared that he will stay in Hong Kong to study politics and law at the University of Hong Kong. Having been exposed to legal matters over the years sparked his interest in law, and he believes 'the law can bring equality and create opportunities.' He therefore hopes to become a barrister in the future, using the law to make legal services accessible to citizens who lack financial resources or are in poor health.

When asked about his thoughts on the current political instability in Hong Kong, Cheng said his 'original intention remains unchanged,' and that social and economic instability would not affect his resolve to pursue a career in law. He believes that 'the law can bring opportunities to people.' As for whether AI will replace legal work, Cheng argued that law requires an understanding of human nature and worldly affairs, and that AI cannot replicate human emotion.

Family support is also crucial along the path of growing up. Cheng's father said, 'He (Cheng) is a very hardworking person,' and believed that Cheng's efforts and the message he conveys can 'encourage those in similar circumstances.' Mr Cheng said, 'All parents hope to see their children grow up healthy.' Upon learning of his son's eye condition, it took him a great deal of time to come to terms with reality, but thankfully he received assistance through channels such as the Ebenezer School & Home for the Visually Impaired.
